tldr: MixReact is a unified framework that generates and controls diverse, physically viable humanoid reactions from text, audio, and video cues. By pairing global discrete-token planning with continuous diffusion state prediction via one-way mixture attention, it prevents mode collapse into averaged behaviors while achieving high-precision closed-loop control.
hero_caption: Overall architecture of MixReact. Text, audio, and video inputs are mapped into semantic memory via MCA. Inside DisCo-MoT, discrete sequence planning and continuous diffusion prediction are combined via one-way Mixture Attention to generate next states. The history-aware controller HAT receives these states to realize robust closed-loop control in a physics simulator.
overview:
In daily life, humans naturally react to surrounding stimuli—ducking an incoming ball or waving back at a greeting. Humanoid agents need similar responsiveness. However, existing reaction generation methods often require special inputs like the conversational partner's 3D skeleton data, or remain confined to purely kinematic generation that ignores physical laws. This causes physical artifacts such as foot sliding, floating, and falls when tracking fails in physics simulators. Furthermore, reaction generation is an inherently one-to-many mapping: a single greeting cue can warrant multiple valid reactions, such as a nod, a wave, or a bow. Continuous representations alone tend to average these behaviors into unnatural, passive poses, while discrete tokens introduce quantization errors that lose the fine-grained details needed for balance.

To tackle these challenges, the authors developed MixReact, a unified framework for physics-based reactive humanoid control from multimodal text, audio, and video cues. At its core is DisCo-MoT, a state prediction model combining the best of discrete and continuous representations. First, a discrete branch samples a token sequence for the entire reaction as a global action plan and caches its intermediate features as Key-Value pairs. Next, a continuous branch references this global context through one-way Mixture Attention and directly predicts future physical states via an autoregressive diffusion model conditioned on past execution history. In addition, the authors integrated HAT, a history-aware action transformer that maps predicted next states and past execution history into executable joint torque commands.

Experiments on the ReactMotionNet (text/audio) and ViMo (video) datasets in the Isaac Gym environment show that MixReact substantially outperforms existing methods across motion fidelity (FID), diversity, and physical consistency (reduced floating and foot-skating errors). It also achieves real-time closed-loop control at roughly 1.15× real-time speed. These results clearly demonstrate the framework's ability to generate and execute diverse, physically stable reactions from multimodal inputs.
contributions: Proposed MixReact, the first unified framework for closed-loop physics-based humanoid reactive control driven by multimodal text, audio, and video inputs.

Introduced the DisCo-MoT architecture, coupling discrete masked modeling and continuous autoregressive diffusion via one-way Mixture Attention to prevent one-to-many averaging collapse while bypassing quantization bottlenecks.
Developed the HAT controller, which integrates predicted states with past execution history to generate joint actions, achieving robust tracking in physics simulation.
Demonstrated superior motion fidelity, diversity, and physical consistency over existing baselines across all three modalities, along with faster-than-real-time control (~1.15× speed).

sections.heading: How can humanoids react naturally to words, sounds, and video?
sections.summary: Humans react in diverse ways to surrounding stimuli, but prior reaction generation focused on kinematic motions assuming access to a partner's 3D motion. This paper targets physically viable humanoid control driven by text, audio, and video cues in physics simulation.
sections.details:
Humans do not move in isolation. When a dog lunges, we flinch back; when a ball flies our way, we guard with our arms; when someone greets us, we wave back. Equipping humanoid agents with this level of flexible responsiveness is a central goal in robotics and Embodied AI.

However, prior reaction generation research faced two major hurdles. First, methods relied on clean 3D skeletal motion from an interaction partner or supported only a single narrow modality such as text or video. Second, the generated motions were purely kinematic (geometric joint angle trajectories) without physical constraints. This led to body interpenetration, foot sliding (skating), and floating. Passing these trajectories directly into a physics simulator caused loss of balance and falls.

An even deeper challenge is that reactions to a stimulus are "one-to-many." For example, upon hearing "Congratulations!", some people clap, while others hug or dance. Conventional continuous modeling tends to blend these distinct reaction modes into an averaged, half-hearted passive pose (mode collapse). Conversely, discrete token modeling can capture diverse modes, but quantization loss strips away the fine-grained physical state details essential for maintaining contact and balance.

Recognizing that "what reaction to perform is a discrete choice, while how to execute it is continuous control," the authors proposed MixReact to integrate both paradigms.

sections.heading: At the crossroads of physics-based humanoid control and multimodal reaction generation
sections.summary: Recent advances span physics-based tracking, diffusion-based motion synthesis, and cue-driven reaction generation. MixReact stands out by eliminating the need for hard-to-acquire 3D partner motions, providing end-to-end closed-loop physical control from multimodal cues.
sections.details:
This work sits at the intersection of three primary research domains:

### Physics-Based Humanoid Control
Reinforcement learning methods for reference motion tracking, such as DeepMimic and AMP, along with robust multi-motion trackers like PHC, have progressed rapidly. Recent efforts like CLoSD combine diffusion planners with controllers to synthesize motions under simulator physical feedback. However, generating one-to-many reactions to multimodal stimuli while ensuring physical viability has remained largely unaddressed.

### Human Reaction Generation
Synthesizing interaction motions traditionally assumed the partner's 3D motion as input. Recently, methods like HERO and NOUS generate reactions from video, while ReactMotion synthesizes listener behaviors from speech text and audio. Yet these remain kinematic; attempting physical execution leads to failure. A few methods attempt physical tracking, but they still require the partner's 3D motion. MixReact operates directly from text, audio, and RGB video without assuming access to difficult-to-capture 3D skeletons in the real world.

### Mixture of Transformers (MoT)
Integrating discrete token prediction and continuous diffusion models within a single Transformer architecture (e.g., Transfusion, MoT) has gained significant attention. DisCo-MoT in MixReact adopts an asymmetric structure: it samples a global reaction plan via discrete masked modeling once and routes those features into the continuous diffusion process through one-way attention.

sections.heading: The DisCo-MoT hybrid architecture and the HAT controller
sections.summary: MixReact consists of MCA (mapping multimodal inputs into semantic memory), DisCo-MoT (connecting discrete global context to continuous diffusion via one-way attention), and HAT (producing torque commands from states and history). Together, they synthesize precise, physically executable state trajectories without averaging collapse.
sections.details:
The entire system is designed as a closed loop from perception to action execution.

### 3.1 Multimodal Context Adapter (MCA)
Features are extracted using pretrained, frozen encoders for text (CLIP), audio (AudioCLIP), and video (TC-CLIP). Modality-specific linear layers and a shared projection layer map these into a unified semantic memory $C$, which conditions DisCo-MoT.

### 3.2 Discrete–Continuous Mixture of Transformers (DisCo-MoT)
DisCo-MoT is the core of this approach and comprises two branches:
- **Discrete Masked-Modeling Branch**: Humanoid state trajectories are pre-quantized into discrete tokens via a VQ-VAE. At the start of inference, a token sequence $Z$ representing the entire reaction is sampled conditioned on the semantic memory $C$. This establishes the high-level reaction strategy (e.g., "clap this time") and remains fixed as a contextual prior across subsequent prediction windows.
- **Continuous Autoregressive Diffusion Branch**: Because directly decoding discrete tokens causes balance loss from quantization errors, this branch predicts future physical states ($D_s=358$ dimensions) directly in continuous space. Conditioned on the past $h_d$ simulation history frames and intermediate features from the discrete branch, it denoises a future $n_f$-frame state window in 10 diffusion steps.
- **One-Way Mixture Attention**: This key design ensures continuous branch queries can attend to their own Key-Values as well as cached Key-Values from the discrete branch, with gradients severed via a stop-gradient operator. Meanwhile, an attention mask prevents the discrete branch from attending to continuous branch representations. This prevents local denoising fluctuations from corrupting the global action plan.

### 3.3 History-Aware Action Transformer (HAT)
HAT takes the predicted next desired state $\hat{s}_{t+1}$ from DisCo-MoT and the recent simulation execution history $H_t^a$ as inputs, outputting target joint angle actions $a_t \in \mathbb{R}^{69}$ for joint PD controllers. Trained via DAgger-based online distillation from a teacher policy (PHC), HAT can compensate for its own tracking errors using historical observations, yielding high disturbance robustness.

captions.F2: Internal processing flow of DisCo-MoT. The top discrete branch generates a global token sequence in one shot, and its intermediate Key-Values guide the bottom continuous autoregressive diffusion branch via one-way attention. Predicted states are passed to HAT on the right, forming a closed loop with feedback history from the simulator.

sections.heading: Outperforming baselines in expressiveness and physical stability
sections.summary: Evaluated on ReactMotionNet and ViMo, MixReact outperformed baselines across FID, diversity, and physical consistency (reduced floating and skating). Ablations confirmed the complementary roles of discrete and continuous representations and the necessity of one-way attention.
sections.details:
Evaluation was conducted on the text/audio dataset ReactMotionNet and the video dataset ViMo within the Isaac Gym simulator, using an SMPL humanoid model with 24 joints and 69 actuators.

### Quantitative Evaluation and Baseline Comparison
MixReact was benchmarked against ReactMotion++, HERO++, and NOUS++ (existing kinematic generators paired with a tracking controller) as well as CLoSD (an integrated diffusion planner and controller, extended for multimodal cues).
- **Motion Quality and Diversity**: MixReact achieved the lowest FID across all modalities, including a 17.5% improvement over NOUS++ on video (ViMo). It also scored highest in MultiModality (MModality), which measures reaction spread for identical stimuli, demonstrating rich one-to-many generation.
- **Physical Consistency**: Skating error (measuring foot sliding) decreased by 34.2% compared to NOUS++, while Floating error decreased by 40.9% compared to ReactMotion++ on audio inputs. Unlike baselines forcing tracking on static kinematic trajectories, MixReact continuously synthesizes future states conditioned on actual simulation history.

### Qualitative Evaluation
As shown in Figures 3–5, MixReact responds to a "victory" cue with claps and light steps, and dances to rhythmic music. When an explosion occurs in a video, it recoils and steps back while maintaining balance. In contrast, baseline methods either fell over when reacting abruptly to the explosion or collapsed into muted, nearly stationary poses.

### Ablation Studies
Experiments confirmed the value of each component:
- **Removing the discrete branch**: Audio MModality dropped by 38.4%, with motions collapsing into muted, averaged behaviors, confirming the discrete tokens' importance for global intention setting.
- **Removing the continuous branch (decoding tokens directly with VQ-VAE)**: FID worsened by 20.1% on video, and foot-contact errors increased, showing the negative impact of quantization errors on physical control.
- **Switching to bidirectional attention**: Motion Jerk roughly doubled and fall rates spiked because gradients from continuous denoising disrupted the discrete representation, verifying the correctness of the one-way attention design.

captions.F4: Comparison of audio-driven reactions. For rhythmic audio stimuli, MixReact performs dynamic stepping without falling. Baselines fail to track vigorous motion and lose balance.
captions.F5: Comparison of video-driven reactions. For an explosion scene (top), MixReact safely recoils and steps backward, whereas other methods lose balance and collapse onto the ground.
captions.F6: Qualitative results of ablation studies. Removing the discrete branch mutes reactions, removing the continuous branch limits motion range, and bidirectional attention causes instability and falls.

sections.heading: Conclusion: A step toward humanoids interacting with everyday environments
sections.summary: MixReact is a unified framework for physics-based humanoid reactive control from text, audio, and video. Linking discrete global planning with continuous diffusion prediction through one-way attention, it achieves both diversity and physical viability.
sections.details:
This paper presented MixReact, a framework that generates and controls human-like, physically valid humanoid reactions to diverse everyday multimodal stimuli.

By uniting discrete high-level action selection with precise continuous state prediction via DisCo-MoT, and driving joints through the history-aware HAT controller, the framework simultaneously resolves one-to-many averaging collapse and physical execution failures.

In addition to quantitative and qualitative gains, the system operates in real time (~1.15× speed). This represents a meaningful step toward non-player characters (NPCs) in gaming/VR/AR, as well as physical AI and humanoid robots collaborating with humans in the real world.

sections.heading: Appendix: Implementation details, user study, real-time performance, and one-to-many behavior
sections.summary: The appendix details HAT's online distillation, a 20-participant user study, computational latency achieving ~1.15× real-time control at 30 Hz, and concrete examples of one-to-many reactions generated from identical cues.
sections.details:
Key takeaways from the paper's appendix provide deeper insight into implementation and reproducibility:

### HAT Online Distillation and Fall Rate Reduction
HAT is trained via DAgger-based online distillation from a frozen tracking teacher policy (PHC). Under states $s_t$ and execution histories $H_t^a$ visited by HAT in the simulator, it imitates the teacher's action $a_t^T$. This history-aware design significantly lowered fall rates compared to directly deploying the PHC teacher (text: 0.82% → 0.30%; video: 18.29% → 15.89%). Fall rates are higher overall on video tasks because ViMo motions involve dynamic center-of-mass shifts.

### User Study and Real-Time Performance
- **User Study**: In a 5-point evaluation across reaction quality and contextual alignment by 20 participants, MixReact scored 4.22 on text, 4.13 on audio, and 4.17 on video, substantially outperforming baselines (the best baseline, NOUS++, reached 3.63, while ReactMotion++ scored in the 2s).
- **Inference Speed**: On a single NVIDIA RTX 3090 GPU, DisCo-MoT requires 52.47 ms for initial discrete plan sampling (reused thereafter) and 79.49 ms to predict a 60-frame state window (2 seconds, equivalent to 754.8 states/s). HAT inference takes only 3.39 ms. End-to-end system throughput including simulation reaches 34.51 steps/s, confirming ~1.15× faster-than-real-time execution against the target 30 Hz control cycle.

### Variations in One-to-Many Reactions
Conditioned on the exact same cue, sampling the discrete branch produces markedly different behaviors. For instance, in response to speech expressing sorrow or regret, the agent can place hands over its face in concern, raise a hand in reassurance, or lean forward attentively—all executed stably in physical simulation while remaining contextually appropriate.

captions.F10: Examples of one-to-many reaction generation. Three distinct reactions generated by MixReact from the same text, audio, or video cue via sampling. All reactions match context while stably executing distinct body motions and posture adjustments in physical simulation.

takeaways: Dividing roles between discrete tokens for 'what to do' (global planning) and continuous diffusion for 'how to move' (fine control) provides a powerful design pattern to simultaneously avoid one-to-many averaging collapse and quantization artifacts.

Restricting information flow from the discrete branch to the continuous branch to be strictly one-way (using stop-gradient and attention masking) prevents local diffusion noise from destabilizing the global behavioral context.

For physical humanoid control, closed-loop designs that continuously feed actual simulator execution history into both the planner (DisCo-MoT) and low-level controller (HAT)—rather than tracking static kinematic trajectories—are critical to preventing falls.
limitations: MixReact does not account for relative 3D spatial positions or physical contact constraints with entities in the cue (e.g., dogs or objects in video), leaving precise physical contact interactions for future work.
Although the framework handles multiple cue modalities, dataset limitations restrict inference to a single modality (text, audio, or video) at a time, preventing simultaneous multimodal conditioning.
Validation is restricted to a physics simulator (Isaac Gym); addressing sensor noise and the Sim-to-Real gap on real humanoid hardware remains an open challenge.
